title: If You Feel Older Than You Are, It Is Probably Ruining Your Sleep. A New Study Explains Why.
excerpt: A study of 3,177 adults found that people who feel older than their chronological age sleep worse, feel worse during the day, and report poorer physical health — a pattern that may hit the overworked Indian diaspora especially hard.
body:
A new study being presented at the SLEEP 2026 annual meeting in Baltimore has uncovered a striking connection between how old a person feels and how well they actually sleep. Adults who perceive themselves as older than their chronological age reported significantly more insomnia symptoms, worse sleep quality, lower sleep regularity, and greater daytime impairment — all of which, in turn, were linked to poorer physical health.

The research team, led by Joseph M. Dzierzewski of the National Sleep Foundation, analysed data from 3,177 adults with an average age of 42.8 years. They calculated something called "age discrepancy" — the gap between how old you feel and how old you actually are. Those who felt older than their years showed consistent deficits across every sleep measure examined, even after adjusting for actual age, sex, race, depression, and anxiety.

## The Mechanism Nobody Talks About

What makes this study particularly compelling is the mediation analysis. The researchers found that feeling older did not just correlate with worse sleep — it was the disrupted sleep itself that appeared to bridge the gap between subjective aging and declining physical health. In other words, feeling old wrecks your sleep, and wrecked sleep wrecks your body. It is a vicious cycle with a clear entry point.

"These findings suggest how people perceive their own aging may have important implications for sleep and overall well-being," Dzierzewski said. "Understanding subjective age could help inform future approaches to support healthier sleep and quality of life across the lifespan."

The study was published as an abstract in the journal *Sleep* and funded by the National Institute on Aging.

## Why This Matters for the Indian Diaspora

For South Asians living abroad, the findings land with particular weight. The immigrant experience — the stress of cultural dislocation, the pressure to provide for families across two countries, long hours in demanding jobs, and the emotional toll of being far from aging parents — can make people feel decades older than they are. Research on South Asian immigrants in the United States has consistently found elevated rates of cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and metabolic syndrome, even in those with seemingly healthy profiles. Now, subjective aging and the sleep disruption it causes may be an overlooked piece of that puzzle.

Indian-origin professionals in the tech, healthcare, and finance sectors are among the most overworked demographics in America. A 2024 survey by the American Psychological Association found that Asian Americans reported the highest levels of work-related burnout among all ethnic groups. When you add immigration-related stressors — visa uncertainty, family responsibilities spanning continents, the silent expectation of success — the result is a generation that may be aging faster in their own minds than their bodies can sustain.

## The Sleep Connection India Already Understands

India's own sleep crisis provides context. A 2023 study published in *The Lancet Regional Health — Southeast Asia* found that nearly 33 per cent of Indian adults suffer from poor sleep quality, with urbanisation, screen time, and work pressure cited as primary drivers. For NRIs who grew up in this culture of chronic underrest and then moved into even more demanding Western work environments, the pattern compounds.

Ayurvedic medicine has long emphasised the link between perceived vitality and sleep quality. The concept of *ojas* — a subtle energy that governs immunity, vigour, and how "young" a person feels — is intimately tied to sleep in classical texts. Modern science is now catching up to what traditional Indian medicine has described for centuries: the feeling of being worn down is not just in your head. It is in your circadian rhythm.

## What You Can Do

The researchers suggest that interventions targeting subjective aging — essentially, helping people feel younger — could have downstream benefits for sleep and physical health. This could include cognitive reframing, regular physical activity, social engagement, and stress management.

For the diaspora, the prescription might be simpler than it sounds. Reconnecting with cultural practices — morning walks, yoga, communal meals, the rhythms of a joint family — may offer more than nostalgia. They may offer a way to feel less old in a world that ages immigrants faster than they should.

The study will be formally presented on June 17 at the Associated Professional Sleep Societies meeting in Baltimore.

*Sources: Journal of Sleep (DOI: 10.1093/sleep/zsag091.0849); American Academy of Sleep Medicine; American Psychological Association; The Lancet Regional Health — Southeast Asia*
